EVAPORATION LOSSES UNDER INTERMITTENT SPRINKLER IRRIGATION IN ARID CONDITIONS: A FIELD STUDY

Journal: Water Conservation and Management (WCM)
Author: Khusnora Khusanbaeva, Sabirjan Isaev, Sunnat Tadjiev, Shokhrukh Azizov, Jamshid Narzullaev, Nematov Ulugbek, Guzal Xonkeldiyeva, Abdukadir Butayarov, Abdukadir Genjemuratov, Bakhtiyor Kamilov, Musulman Ziyatov, Farrukh Abdikulov

ABSTRACT

Sprinkler irrigation loses a substantial share of applied water to wind drift and evaporation (WDEL) before it ever reaches the crop root zone, and this loss is especially severe under arid and semi-arid conditions. In the Tashkent region of Uzbekistan, we compared WDEL under intermittent and continuous sprinkler operation, using a center-pivot system held at constant hydraulic settings across 25 field runs. We measured collected water depth with the catch-can method and tracked wind speed, air temperature, and relative humidity throughout each run. Intermittent operation cut WDEL by roughly 20–30% relative to continuous operation under otherwise comparable weather, a reduction that held consistently across the growing season. A power-law model linking WDEL to air density predicted losses with good accuracy (R² = 0.866, RMSE = 0.71%, mean relative error ≈ 3.7%). These results show that how irrigation is scheduled in time — not just how much water is applied — shapes evaporation losses in the field, a factor that current sprinkler management and modeling practices still tend to overlook.
